Two properties are in play, and they pull in different directions. Conductivity is how fast heat moves through the metal. Heat capacity is how much heat the metal holds at a given temperature. Aluminum wins on the first. Cast iron wins on the second, mostly because a typical skillet is far heavier.

A 10-inch cast-iron skillet weighs around five pounds. A thin aluminum pan of the same width might weigh one. At the same temperature, the iron pan stores several times more heat, simply because there is more metal to store it in.

Now put a cold steak on each. The aluminum pan spreads heat evenly and quickly, but it has little in reserve. The steak pulls heat out, the pan's surface temperature drops, and the burner has to catch up. The iron pan's surface dips less, because the thick body keeps feeding heat to the steak. That is why the sear stays hard and the crust browns instead of the meat turning gray and steaming.

The limitation: cast iron conducts poorly, so it heats unevenly. A small burner leaves a hot spot under the flame and cooler edges. Staying hot is not the same as heating evenly.

Here's the thing people get tangled up on: conducting heat and holding heat are two different jobs. Aluminum is a fantastic conductor, so heat zips through it fast. But it's also light, and a light pan simply doesn't have much stuff in it to store energy. Cast iron is a mediocre conductor, yet it's heavy, and all that mass acts like a battery. More iron means more stored heat.

Picture dropping two cold steaks into two pans that were both preheated to the same temperature. The thin aluminum pan heats up evenly in seconds, but the moment cold meat hits it, the temperature plunges, and there's not much reserve to bounce back. You get gray, steamy edges. The cast-iron pan dips a little, too, but it has so much stored heat to draw on that the surface stays hot enough to build a real crust. That's why I'll always grab iron for searing (and why my aluminum skillet is relegated to eggs).

The limitation? Iron's slow conduction means it heats unevenly. Put it on a small burner and you'll get a hot spot in the middle while the edges lag, so you've got to preheat patiently. Heavy doesn't automatically mean better.

I paid $38 for this used mechanical keyboard, and I'm keeping it, though not without complaints.

The space bar rattles. Every press produces a hollow clatter, like a pencil dropped in a tin cup, and I hear it most during quiet evening typing. I haven't opened the keyboard to check the stabilizer, so I can't say whether it's a loose wire or just worn plastic.

The other flaw is the "k" key. Maybe once or twice an hour it repeats itself, so "okay" becomes "okkkay." It never happens when I'm watching for it. I've learned to scan each paragraph before sending anything.

What kept me from returning it is how it feels over a long session. I wrote forty emails in one afternoon, and my wrists didn't ache. The keys have enough travel that I stop pressing hard, and the board sits flat without needing a wrist rest.

I asked the seller which switches were inside. The answer came a week later, long after I'd stopped waiting, and it was a single line naming a switch type. By then I had already decided to keep it.

For $38, the noise and the stuttering are annoying but livable. The comfort is real, and it's why this thing stays on my desk.

Thirty-eight bucks. That's what I paid, and honestly, that number explains most of how I feel about this keyboard.

Let's get the bad stuff out of the way. The space bar rattles. Not a gentle clack, either. It's a loose, tinny sound, like a spoon in an empty drawer. And the J key repeats sometimes, just often enough that I've typed "jjust" in three separate emails to my landlord, who probably thinks I'm losing it.

I asked the seller what switches it had before I bought it. He answered a week later. A *week*. By then the thing was already on my desk and I'd figured out they were browns by pulling a keycap and squinting. His reply was one word: "brown." Thanks, man.

But here's the thing. I write long emails for work, the kind that go on forever, and this keyboard is genuinely comfortable for that. My wrists don't ache by the end of the day. The keys have this soft little bump that makes typing feel almost pleasant.

So I kept it. Shipping it back would've eaten a chunk of what I paid, and I'd rather just live with the rattle. Three and a half stars.

The book drop was a milk crate by the back door, and every Thursday around two, Imre found something in it that wasn't milk. First week: *A Field Guide to Mushrooms of the Northeast*, Carver Street Library stamp on the flyleaf, due date long past. Second week, the same book. Third week, the same.

He'd stopped reshelving it in his head. It lived on the flour bench now, between the scale and the tub of rye starter, its cover gone soft with dough-dusted thumbprints.

Tonight he slid the crate out with his hip, hands still in oven mitts, and the book was there again, heavier than usual. A yellow square of paper stuck out near page 112.

He peeled off the mitts. The note was in pencil, small, slanted hard to the right.

*Your door smells better than the library. I keep meaning to bring it to the right place. Is the morel on this page the one you use? —T.*

Imre looked at the page. Someone had circled nothing; the morel sat there, wrinkled and brown.

He pulled the pencil from behind his ear, flipped the note over, and wrote *No. Never used one.* Then, after a moment, he added *Come at five, there's bread.* He pressed it back into the book.

The listing said "minor wear." I paid $38 for a used board with blue switches because my wrists were killing me. It arrived in a box stuffed with grocery bags.

The space bar rattles like a screen door in a storm. So does the right shift, but I use the left one. One key repeats. The E. I'll type "thee" and delete the extra letter. I've done it four times today.

I messaged the seller about the switches the day I bought it. He replied a week later. "They're Gateron blues, I think." Thanks.

I thought about shipping it back. The return label was going to cost me $12, and the seller had already gone quiet again. So I kept it. It's heavy in a good way, and the keys travel far enough that my fingers don't bottom out anymore. I wrote three long emails this morning and my hands didn't ache once.

The rattle I can live with. The E is annoying but survivable. Thirty-eight dollars, and it does the one thing I needed.

I now live in Toronto and no longer use Hydro Ottawa, but I want to warn other consumers about their alarming billing practices. 

I previously held an account for one year while renting a downtown apartment. When I moved back in with my parents to pursue an MA, I officially cancelled my account and paid all outstanding charges. 

Despite the cancellation, Hydro Ottawa continued siphoning payments from my separate bank account at random intervals for over a year. I repeatedly phoned customer service and sent proof of the withdrawals, but representatives insisted my account was closed and that no debits were occurring. 

The truth emerged only when my parents and I cross-referenced our utility bills: Hydro Ottawa had mistakenly linked my banking details to my parents’ billing number simply because I had mentioned moving home. My parents had not noticed because they frequently received overpayment refunds, making the credits seem normal. 

After hours on the phone and speaking with multiple representatives, a manager finally investigated, confirmed the error, and addressed it. Shockingly, they initially refused a refund and offered only an apology. 

I will never again provide banking details for automatic debit. Hydro Ottawa’s reckless handling of customers’ personal data should deeply concern everyone.

Aluminum conducts heat faster, but staying hot depends on a different property: how much heat a pan can store. That's heat capacity, and it depends on how much material you have. A cast-iron skillet is thick and heavy, often 4 to 5 pounds, while a thin aluminum pan might weigh under a pound. Even though aluminum itself holds more heat per pound than iron, the cast-iron pan has far more mass, so it stores much more total heat.

Conductivity mostly affects how quickly and evenly heat spreads. Aluminum heats up fast and responds quickly when you turn the burner down, which also means it loses heat quickly once food hits it.

Here's a kitchen example: you preheat both pans to the same temperature and lay in two cold steaks. The thin aluminum pan's temperature drops sharply because it has little stored heat to give up, and the steaks may start to steam instead of sear. The cast-iron pan dips less, recovers faster, and keeps browning.

One limitation: this comparison isn't perfectly fair if the pans differ in size, thickness, or burner contact. A thick aluminum pan could store plenty of heat too, and cast iron can develop hot spots because it spreads heat less evenly.

Aluminum conducts heat better than cast iron, so heat moves through an aluminum pan more quickly. That helps the pan respond fast when you turn the burner up or down. But staying hot is not just about how fast heat moves. It also depends on how much heat the pan can store.

A typical cast-iron skillet is much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. That extra mass acts like a heat reservoir. Once it is fully preheated, it contains more stored heat, so its temperature drops more slowly when you add cold food.

For example, put a room-temperature steak in a hot cast-iron skillet and in a thin aluminum pan. The steak pulls heat out of both pans. The thin aluminum pan may transfer heat into the steak quickly at first, but it has less stored heat, so its surface temperature can fall fast. The cast iron may conduct heat less efficiently, but because it is heavy, it can keep feeding heat into the steak and maintain a stronger sear.

One limitation: this comparison depends on the actual pans. A thick aluminum griddle can store plenty of heat, and a small, thin cast-iron pan may not. Burner size and preheating time also matter.

Quick take on *Awakening* at Wynn Las Vegas: it’s fine, but not the Vegas must-see I’d build a trip around.

I’ve been taken to Las Vegas constantly since I was a kid—saw a ton of shows before I turned 21—so I’ve got a decent baseline for what these productions can be.

Good news: the circular stage is genuinely smart. From basically any seat, you get a decent view, which is rare in these big theater shows. If you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, there’s a solid deal: tickets normally $125 are $99 for hotel guests. That helps.

Some individual acts are impressive, and the performers are clearly strong as hell—aerialists, acrobats, whatever. But a lot of the feats feel like things I’ve seen done just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows.

The bigger problem is the story. It’s unclear, weak, or practically nonexistent; I left not really knowing what the production was trying to say. There’s also too much going on at once—too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many “wow” attempts. A more restrained production would hit harder.

Aside from a few cool stunts, the whole thing felt average. I wasn’t blown away, and no one I was with seemed overwhelmed either. A few friends did enjoy it, so if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out—especially with the Wynn/Encore deal. But I wouldn’t see it again or pay full price a second time. It tries to be the stereotypical huge, flashy Vegas spectacle where more equals better. More just meant messier for me.
